clue.text: It will be useful, I'll be bound, said this Firebringer

definitions.text: It will be useful, I'll be bound, said this Firebringer

parts.words: It will be useful, I'll be bound, said this Firebringer
parts.note: the Titan who stole fire for mankind, chained to a rock in Aeschylus's play, his name meaning forethought: the one who foresaw fire's usefulness and was bound for it

explanation.surface: A boastful promise, sealed with 'I'll be bound', from the god who brought fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll be bound' is both an idiom for 'I'm sure' and a nod to Aeschylus's play about the chained fire-thief; his name means foresight.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titan stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans, so he is the Firebringer.

clue.text: Sheridan's PR man

parts.note: in Sheridan's comedy The Critic a character is a professional writer of advertising blurbs, named after the word for an inflated notice

explanation.surface: A playwright's publicist.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Critic, Sheridan's character Mr Puff makes his living writing flattering notices, the eighteenth-century equivalent of public relations.

clue.text: Poet in audio-video game …

indicators.note: in says the poet's name sits inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: A poet appearing in some electronic game.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs across the join of audiO VIDeo; 'game' just completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman author of the Metamorphoses is one of the great classical poets.

clue.text: … yet somehow a short time reasoning on dictionary showing roots

indicators.note: somehow says the three letters of yet are to be arranged in some other way

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a short time
logic is reasoning
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the poet's verse is reasoned briefly on a dictionary of word origins.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from the poet clue, but the pieces stand alone here: 'a short time' is crossword shorthand for a moment, and 'somehow' scrambles only the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: An etymologicon is an old word for an etymological dictionary, one that traces where words come from.

clue.text: Dickens wrote that of London

parts.note: a title naming the centre of the capital, the city's core or innermost part, a phrase associated with Dickens

explanation.surface: Something Dickens wrote about London.
explanation.definitionFit: The heart of a city is its central, vital core; 'The Heart of London' names the middle of the capital.

clue.text: Where secondary characters are buried

parts.note: buried reads as lying beneath a grave plot, while a story's minor characters live in its subsidiary storyline

explanation.surface: A graveyard for minor characters in fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as UNDER PLOT, it is where a buried body lies; as one word it is a subplot, home of secondary characters.
explanation.definitionFit: A subsidiary storyline in a play or novel, running beneath the main action, is where minor characters do their work.

clue.text: Guide to Montague's city provided by Henry Reed?

definitions.text: Guide to Montague's city provided by Henry Reed?

parts.words: Guide to Montague's city provided by Henry Reed?
parts.note: Romeo Montague's city is Verona, and the poet Henry Reed titled a poem and collection after a chart of that city

explanation.surface: A tourist guide to Verona written by a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Reed, the poet of 'Naming of Parts', published 'A Map of Verona'; Verona is the home of Shakespeare's Montagues.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart of a city is a guide to it, and Reed's poem names one of Verona.

clue.text: The kind of female liable to wear caps by night" (Frederick Rolfe)

definitions.text: The kind of female liable to wear caps by night" (Frederick Rolfe)

parts.words: The kind of female liable to wear caps by night" (Frederick Rolfe)
parts.note: a quotation from Frederick Rolfe (Baron Corvo) describing a type of woman by the Scottish queen in her famous cap

explanation.surface: A quotation describing a type of woman given to nightcaps.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen of Scots is known from portraits in a distinctive heart-shaped cap; Rolfe's phrase names the type after her.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixteenth-century Queen of Scots was famously painted in a close-fitting cap, so her name labels the cap-wearing type of woman.

clue.text: Some of his cast seem to have found him elusive

definitions.text: Some of his cast seem to have found him elusive

parts.words: Some of his cast seem to have found him elusive
parts.note: the dramatist's best-known play has six characters searching in vain for their author

explanation.surface: Actors struggling to track down their elusive playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Six Characters in Search of an Author' part of the cast literally hunts for the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian dramatist wrote 'Six Characters in Search of an Author', whose characters never find the man who made them.

clue.text: Dylan's fair version of little people's homes

indicators.note: a version of something is a reworking, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the name with its possessive s supplies its letters as written

explanation.surface: Dylan Thomas's own take on the land of the little folk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version' rearranges DYLANS and FAIR together; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The realms where fairies, the 'little people' of folklore, are imagined to live.

clue.text: Close relation from the South, possibly a hero for Updike

definitions.text: Close relation from the South, possibly a hero for Updike

parts.words: Close relation from the South, possibly a hero for Updike
parts.note: a Southern US dialect word for a sibling, and the title of a folk-tale rabbit, while Updike's hero is Rabbit Angstrom

explanation.surface: A Southern relative who might star in an Updike novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The dialect title of Brer Rabbit in the Uncle Remus tales; Updike's novels follow Harry 'Rabbit' Angstrom, hence 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Southern US dialect for a sibling, best known from Brer Rabbit, whose nickname Updike's hero shares.

clue.text: "c'est moi" (Flaubert)

parts.note: Flaubert is said to have answered questions about his heroine's model by saying she was himself

explanation.surface: Flaubert's famous admission of identity.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaubert reputedly declared his heroine was himself: the full saying begins with her name and ends 'c'est moi'.

clue.text: Straight man of Baker Street

parts.note: the comedian's foil at 221B Baker Street is the detective's companion and narrator

explanation.surface: The comic's foil in a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Sherlock Holmes lived at 221B Baker Street; his companion plays the plain foil to his brilliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Holmes's companion and chronicler serves as the dependable foil to the detective, as a comedian's partner does.

clue.text: The world of Powell

parts.note: Anthony Powell titled the third novel of A Dance to the Music of Time with a word placed before world

explanation.surface: The milieu of a novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Powell's novel is 'The Acceptance World', a phrase for the realm of trust and credit.

clue.text: One of three unattractive choices for The Lion in Winter

definitions.text: One of three unattractive choices for The Lion in Winter

parts.words: One of three unattractive choices for The Lion in Winter
parts.note: in the play Henry II, the ageing lion, must choose an heir among his three sons, the youngest being sulky and feeble

explanation.surface: An ageing king weighing three poor options.
explanation.walkthrough: In James Goldman's play Henry II weighs Richard, Geoffrey and the youngest son as successors.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry II's youngest son, later King of England, is one of the three heirs the king finds unappealing in the play.

clue.text: Bodily makeover for poor Clare

indicators.note: a makeover remodels something, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A physical transformation for a poor woman called Clare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makeover' rearranges POOR CLARE; 'for' is a link. A Poor Clare is also a nun, misleading the reader.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a physical body rather than a spiritual one; both words mean of the flesh.

clue.text: Poet's strange device

parts.note: Longfellow's poem has a youth carrying a banner 'with the strange device', a Latin word meaning higher

explanation.surface: An odd gadget belonging to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'device' means the motto on a banner, not a gadget; Longfellow's youth bears 'a banner with the strange device'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin motto, meaning 'ever upward', is the strange device on the banner in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: An attractive accent

parts.note: cute means attractive

explanation.surface: Someone with a charming way of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: The rising mark over a vowel, as in café, is one of the diacritic marks.

clue.text: Trouble in French literature from some poison-pen nuisance

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An anonymous letter-writer stirring up trouble in French books.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across poison-pEN NUIsance.
explanation.definitionFit: Listless boredom, a malaise central to nineteenth-century French writing such as Baudelaire's.

clue.text: Poetic-crime scene

parts.note: T. S. Eliot's verse drama sets the murder of Thomas Becket in a great church

explanation.surface: Where a crime in verse took place.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's 'Murder in the Cathedral' is a play in verse about Becket's killing at Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's verse play places Becket's murder inside the great church at Canterbury.

clue.text: Fowles book suggests the pass to Hannibal

parts.note: taken as written
a col is a mountain pass

indicators.note: suggests here means the word is only hinted at by its sound, matching a cannibal's surname

parts.note: Hannibal Lecter is the serial killer of Thomas Harris's novels

explanation.surface: A novel hints at Hannibal's crossing of the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: Hannibal seems to be the Carthaginian general crossing an Alpine pass; really he is Lecter, whose surname 'suggests' the end of the title. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: John Fowles's first novel, about a man who kidnaps a woman, is 'The Collector'.

clue.text: What we shall play if it rains, suggested Eliot

definitions.text: What we shall play if it rains, suggested Eliot

parts.words: What we shall play if it rains, suggested Eliot
parts.note: in The Waste Land: 'if it rains, a closed car at four. And we shall play a game of' the board game

explanation.surface: A wet-weather plan proposed by a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Section II of The Waste Land, titled 'A Game of Chess', has the speaker plan this board game for a rainy day.

clue.text: Philosopher initiates historical undertaking most effectively

indicators.note: initiates means begins, so take the first letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: A thinker launches a history project with great efficiency.
explanation.walkthrough: David Hume, the Scottish philosopher, also wrote a celebrated History of England, which gives the surface its point.
explanation.definitionFit: David Hume was the eighteenth-century Scottish empiricist thinker.

clue.text: Where The Eagle Has Landed

parts.note: the title of Jack Higgins's thriller, read literally, is a bird of prey alighting at its high nest

explanation.surface: The setting of a wartime thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to Higgins's novel, but read literally an eagle lands on its nest.
explanation.definitionFit: A variant spelling of eyrie, the lofty nest of an eagle, where the bird comes to rest.

clue.text: When to see purple glow on Irish isle

definitions.text: When to see purple glow on Irish isle

parts.words: When to see purple glow on Irish isle
parts.note: Yeats's Lake Isle of Innisfree has 'midnight's all a glimmer, and' midday 'a purple glow'

explanation.surface: The best time to view a glowing light on an island in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats writes that on Innisfree midday is 'a purple glow', the heather lit by the sun.

clue.text: French bed time: true distortion of work of imagination

parts.note: lit is French for bed
an era is a period of time

indicators.note: distortion twists the letters of true into another order

explanation.surface: In France, bedtime stories are a twisted version of truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distortion' turns TRUE into TURE; 'of' and the colon are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Imaginative writing such as novels and poems; a single creative work can be called a piece of it.

clue.text: New dean as seen by giant writer

indicators.note: new means freshly made, so these letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A new dean viewed by a very tall author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giant' is not size: Edna Ferber wrote the novel Giant. 'as seen by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Edna Ferber was the author of the novel 'Giant', later filmed with James Dean.

clue.text: Lord hear my earnest cry and prayer

definitions.text: Lord hear my earnest cry and prayer

parts.words: Lord hear my earnest cry and prayer
parts.note: Burns's Holy Willie's Prayer begins 'Lord, hear my earnest cry and pray'r' against the church court of Ayr

explanation.surface: A heartfelt prayer to God.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns's 'Holy Willie's Prayer' asks the Lord to hear his plea 'against that Presbyt'ry o' Ayr'.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's satirical prayer is aimed at the Ayr church court of elders, a body governing Scottish parishes.
